rv.q: It is a penetrating production, lean, charged, and fresh
A chorus of women plead with her — “why let grief eat you alive?” they sing — and her sister Chrysothemis (Marième Diouf) picks her way through the dark to reason with her.

Where the Old Vic’s Rami Malek-fronted Oedipus was over-conceptualised into oblivion, Daniel Fish’s take on Elektra – which opened one night later – is a curious mixture of chaotic randomness and underlying respect for the 2,500-year-old play. Marvel star Brie Larson puts in a very solid turn as the eponymous princess.
It’s a fascinating experiment, one that’s beautiful, but ultimately impenetrable.

Larson certainly manifests a focus and commitment that suggests she wasn’t crazy to undertake the role, even if she falls short of previous luminaries (10 years ago we had Kristin Scott Thomas; a generation before that, Zoë Wanamaker). The current wave of visiting Hollywood names seems drawn to unyielding, obstinate characters.
You’ll follow the plot, pretty much, without quite knowing why you should care.

It is so self-consciously stylised, so artful and so devoid of any genuine sense of humanity in extremis that it’s more likely to provoke a yawn or a weary eye roll than pity or terror. You sense that it’s straining for austere elegance and intellectual heft; it comes off simply as sterile and insufferably pretentious.
The effect is to turn the piece into an abstract meditation rather than drama
...a production designed to stretch its audience and it won’t be to everyone’s taste
Atmosphere is mere ornamentation...coiled at the heart of the play
